p45: 45.  The Court notes that in the present case the applicant, who is of Roma origin, alleged that a book and two dictionaries funded by the State contained remarks and expressions that were hostile to Roma. He considered that these remarks amounted to an attack on his Roma identity. However, the Court observes that no difference in treatment, and in particular no issue of ethnic discrimination, is at stake in the present case, as the applicant has failed to adduce prima facie evidence that the impugned publications had a discriminatory intent or effect. The case is therefore not comparable to other cases previously lodged by members of the Roma community (see, in the field of education, ibid., §§ 175-210; in the field of housing, Chapman v. the United Kingdom [GC], no. 27238/95, § 73, ECHR 2001-I; and, in the electoral field, Sejdić and Finci v. Bosnia and Herzegovina [GC], nos. 27996/06 and 34836/06, § 45, ECHR 2009). Accordingly, the main issue in the present case is whether the impugned publications, which according to the applicant contained racially insulting remarks, infringed the applicant’s right to respect for his private life and, if so, whether that infringement was compatible with Article 8 of the Convention. The Court will therefore examine the present case solely under that provision.
p46: 46.  The Government disputed the applicant’s victim status in both applications, arguing that they amounted to an actio popularis. In the Government’s view, the applicant had not shown that he had been directly affected by the impugned remarks and expressions.
p47: 47.  The applicant argued that, on account of his Roma/Gypsy origin, he had sustained pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage as a result of the remarks and expressions in the book and dictionaries in question, which in his view were debasing. He therefore considered that he had victim status under Article 34 of the Convention.
p48: 48.  In the view of the Greek Helsinki Monitor, any member of an ethnic group targeted by remarks expressing general discrimination based on race had victim status, given that such expressions generated prejudice against each member of that group. The Greek Helsinki Monitor further considered that the protection afforded by the Court could not be less than that provided by the domestic system: the acceptance of victim status at domestic level should entail recognition of that status by the Court.
p49: 49.  The Chamber observed that, although the applicant had not been directly and personally targeted either in the book or in the two dictionaries in question, he had been able to bring compensation proceedings and to plead his case before the domestic courts on the basis of the provisions of domestic law, namely Articles 24 and 25 of the Civil Code (see paragraph 35 above). Accordingly, the Chamber considered that the applicant had victim status under Article 34 of the Convention.
p50: 50.  The Court reiterates that, in order to be able to lodge an application in accordance with Article 34 of the Convention, a person, non-governmental organisation or group of individuals must be able to claim to be the victim of a violation of the rights set forth in the Convention. In order to claim to be a victim of a violation, a person must be directly affected by the impugned measure. The Convention does not, therefore, envisage the bringing of an actio popularis for the interpretation of the rights set out therein; nor does it permit individuals to complain about a provision of national law simply because they consider, without having been directly affected by it, that it may contravene the Convention (see Burden, cited above, § 33, and Tănase v. Moldova [GC], no. 7/08, § 104, ECHR 2010).
p51: 51.  Accordingly, the existence of a victim who was personally affected by the alleged violation of a Convention right is indispensable for putting the protection mechanism of the Convention into motion, although this criterion is not to be applied in a rigid and inflexible way (see Bitenc v. Slovenia (dec.), no. 32963/02, 18 March 2008). The question whether or not an applicant can claim to be a victim of the violation alleged is relevant at all stages of the proceedings under the Convention (see Bourdov v. Russia, no. 59498/00, § 30, ECHR 2002-III).
p52: 52.  The Court reiterates that it interprets the concept of victim autonomously and irrespective of domestic concepts such as those concerning an interest or capacity to act (see Sanles Sanles v. Spain (dec.), no. 48335/99, ECHR 2000-XI), even though the Court should have regard to the fact that an applicant was a party to the domestic proceedings (see Micallef v. Malta [GC], no. 17056/06, § 48, ECHR 2009).
